newsitem.title: HONG KONG: May election set for Chinese-ruled Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: May election set for Chinese-ruled Hong Kong.

text.p: On the eve of Chinese rule, Hong Kong's future chief executive Tung Chee-hwa on Sunday set a timetable for elections and China's President Jiang Zemin pledged to uphold human rights and freedom.
Tung told visiting Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer that elections for a new legislature would be held next May, Downer told reporters.
The shipping magnate chosen by Beijing to bridge the handover after 156 years of British colonial rule had earlier promised a vote within a year. But he had not named the month.
"Mr Tung gave me a guarantee that those elections would take place... and he expected the elections would take place in May of next year," Downer said.

Hong Kong's democratically-elected legislative council, Britain's parting political gift to its territory and the focus of bitter Sino-British feuding -- will be replaced hours after the midnight Monday (1600 GMT) handover with a provisional legislature appointed by Beijing. Several of the territory's most popular lawmakers lose their places.
Jiang vowed at a ceremony in Beijing's Great Hall of the People to implement strictly promises China made under a 1984 agreement handing Hong Kong back to Chinese rule.

"We will firmly uphold the principles of 'one country, two systems' and 'Hong Kong people governing Hong Kong' as well as a high degree of autonomy," Jiang was quoted as saying by the official Xinhua news agency.
China would "safeguard the Hong Kong residents' rights and freedoms in accordance with the law".

Streets in the Chinese capital were festooned with banners proclaiming "Wash away 100 years of national shame", and a blimp floating high over the city carried the message "Celebrate the return of Hong Kong".
A carnival atmosphere was building in Hong Kong, where heir to the British throne Prince Charles handed out the last colonial knighthoods and honours in the gilded ballroom of Government House.
Bauhinia flower flags of the new Hong Kong trailed from radio antennae of taxis and Union Jacks fluttered from the balconies of British expatriate homes.

British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook vowed to defend London's democratic legacy, and if necessary rally international support. U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright also pledged Washington's vigilance.

Chiding Beijing again over its decision to assert sovereignty swiftly by sending in 4,000 troops and armour at dawn of day one of its rule, Cook said London would keep China to its promise to hold popular elections.
"The people of Hong Kong have now had a taste of democracy. It must be a prime objective of British policy to make sure that taste does not become a memory," he told reporters.

Albright, visiting Hong Kong along with a host of dignitaries to attend end-of-empire pageantry and partying, said: "We expect officials in Beijing and Hong Kong to respect the freedoms of Hong Kong people.
"We will closely watch to see if free and fair elections for a new legislature are conducted as promised at an early date."

Departing Governor Chris Patten attacked "demeaning, patronising, mule-headed" arguments against democracy in the territory, whose new leaders have stressed stability and prosperity ahead of individual freedoms.
He lambasted a "small band of self-appointed good-mouthers who tell the world that Hong Kongers don't care about democracy and civil liberties but only about making money".
In a radio address, he said demonstrators who take to the streets each June 4 to mark the anniversary of the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre in Beijing "gave an eloquent answer to that nonsense".
Patten's crusade for one-man-one-vote in Hong Kong plunged relations between Britain and China into crisis.
As he welcomed individually a series of world leaders, Tung made clear democratic feedoms in Hong Kong would have limits.

He said in a radio interview that while he had no objection to protesters burning his effigy, attacks on Beijing leaders and advocacy of independence for Taiwan and Tibet -- regarded by Beijing as seditious acts -- would be another matter.
In India, the office of Tibet's exiled spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, predicted on Saturday that Hong Kong was doomed to the same fate as Tibet.
Chinese rulers could not be trusted to keep their promises, a statement said. "Human rights and democracy will be the first casualty of reunification with China," it predicted.

To avoid any risk of encountering demonstrators, Jiang and Chinese Premier Li Peng are due to sail across Victoria Harbour to Hong Kong island late on Monday to receive the colony back from Prince Charles.
Tung has warned pro-democracy activists against staging a protest on the balcony of the legislature building while Beijing-appointed lawmakers were being sworn in.
Under controversial laws prepared by the new legislature and due to come into force at midnight, police approval will be required to stage protests.
Political rows were forgotton or ignored by Hong Kong residents on Sunday, as a bright sun illuminated the twilight of imperial rule.
It was a harbinger of hope for superstitious Hong Kongers, though weather experts said the typhoon season might yet dump rain on the final parades and flourishes on Monday.

Chinese families posed for souvenir pictures in front of the Britannia, moored on the Victoria Harbour waterfront, and outside Government House, where Britain's royal coat of arms will soon be removed from the gates.
